name: Procyanidin oral (melasma)

chain: Antioxidant pill with vitamins A, C, E
angle.text: Users take oral procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E to fade melasma patches and even out facial skin tone from the inside. It has been tested in one small 8-week placebo-controlled trial in women with epidermal melasma; larger studies have not been reported.

summary: An antioxidant pill combo with one small placebo-controlled melasma trial reported, and little else.
note: Evidence rests on a single 56-person trial as summarized on Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
This is a supplement combining procyanidin, a plant polyphenol, with vitamins A, C and E, tested for melasma.
One 8-week placebo-controlled trial in 56 women reported improvement on the cheeks. No other studies were found.
How it works: The sources reviewed do not describe how it would act; antioxidant activity is the usual proposed basis for such combinations.
Risks and caveats: The trial summary describes the regimen as safe and well tolerated. Long-term safety data were not found.
deepLead:
Oral procyanidin combined with vitamins A, C and E is a supplement regimen that has been tested for melasma, a facial hyperpigmentation disorder. Wikipedia's melasma article lists it among oral options, citing an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 56 Filipino women with epidermal melasma .
That trial reportedly found significant improvement in the malar (cheek) regions, and the treatment was described as safe and well tolerated . The sources reviewed contain only this one summary, with no independent replication.

name: Quinine skin lightener

angle.text: Quinine has turned up as an ingredient in illicit skin-lightening products sold for a paler complexion, alongside steroids and mercury compounds. Its use for skin tone is based on product reports and enforcement records; it has not been studied as a lightener.

summary: An antimalarial alkaloid reported in illicit lightening products, with no studies of it for skin tone.
note: Associated with the illegal lightening market; no efficacy or safety studies found.
currentQuick:
Quinine is mentioned as an ingredient found in some illegal skin-lightening products, alongside steroids and mercury compounds.
No studies of it as a skin lightener were found.
How it works: No mechanism for skin lightening is described in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Products in the illicit market are reported to contain hazardous ingredients such as mercury and potent steroids, and regulators in several countries have acted against them. Quinine-specific harms in this use were not documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Quinine has been reported as an ingredient in some skin-lightening products sold illegally, alongside corticosteroids, mercury compounds and bleach-based preparations . Wikipedia's skin whitening article mentions it in the context of a 1997 Paris police crackdown on illegal trafficking of such products .
The sources reviewed give no information on how quinine would lighten skin, on any trials, or on its specific harms in this use.

name: Lead-based ceruse

angle.text: Ceruse was a white face paste used for centuries to give a pale, even complexion and cover blemishes, scars and freckles. The whitening was immediately visible, and pale skin signalled wealth and leisure. It is documented as a historical cosmetic rather than a modern option.

summary: A historical lead-based white face paste that whitened skin and poisoned its users.
note: Contains lead; documented to cause lead poisoning.
currentQuick:
Ceruse was a white paste made from lead, used from antiquity to the 18th century to give a pale complexion and cover blemishes. Venetian ceruse was the most prized version.
It is a historical practice rather than a current product, documented here because it is a well-known example of a lightening agent with serious harms.
How it works: The paste was applied to the face as an opaque white cover, with lead-containing pigment suspended in vinegar or similar carriers. It masked skin tone rather than altering melanin.
Risks and caveats: Historical accounts describe lead poisoning from skin absorption, with abdominal pain, organ damage, convulsions and death, plus skin damage that led to heavier application. The WHO lists lead as a major cosmetic chemical of concern.
deepLead:
Ceruse, also called Venetian ceruse or white lead, was a cosmetic paste of lead carbonate used for centuries to whiten the face and cover blemishes, scars and freckles, often prepared with vinegar. Pale skin signalled wealth and leisure in the societies that used it, since outdoor labourers tanned.
Repeated application allowed lead to be absorbed through the skin, and historical accounts describe poisoning, organ damage and death among users. It is no longer a legitimate cosmetic; the World Health Organization listed lead as a major chemical of concern in cosmetics in 2010.

name: Pearl extract

angle.text: Pearl extract and powder are used in traditional Chinese medicine and in cosmetics marketed for brightening and anti-aging. Appearance claims rest on a long tradition and mostly laboratory-level findings, with few human skin trials.

summary: A traditional pearl-derived brightening ingredient with a 2,000-year pedigree and mostly lab-level evidence.
note: Human trials for appearance outcomes are scarce.
currentQuick:
Pearl extract is made from ground pearls or nacre and is used in traditional Chinese medicine and in brightening and anti-aging skin care. Its use is documented for well over a thousand years.
Research is mostly in cells and animals, with a few papers on lightening and melasma. Controlled human trials for appearance are limited.
How it works: Laboratory papers propose antioxidant effects, support for fibroblast migration and, in one report, antagonism of endothelin as a route to skin lightening.
Risks and caveats: Sources describe it as widely used topically; Wikipedia notes oral doses in traditional medicine and that excessive amounts may cause calcium toxicity. Little safety data from controlled skin trials was found.
deepLead:
Pearl extract and pearl powder are preparations made from pearls or nacre, used in traditional Chinese medicine and in cosmetics marketed for brightening and anti-aging. Pearl medicine in China has a history of more than 2,000 years, and it is described as used to calm the mind, clear the eyes and soothe skin.
Published research on pearl extract in skin applications consists largely of laboratory and animal studies, such as work on fibroblast migration, UV-exposed skin cells and photoaging in mice, along with a small number of reports on skin lightening and melasma. Evidence from controlled human trials for appearance outcomes is limited.

name: Fermented rice water (sake lees)

angle.text: Sake lees is used in J-beauty masks, creams and bath powders for a brighter, moisturized complexion. Users report a glow after use, and laboratory work has found tyrosinase-inhibiting activity; controlled human trials of its brightening effect are limited.

summary: Pressed sake residue used in J-beauty masks for brightening, backed by user reports and a tyrosinase-inhibitor finding.
note: Contains alcohol; no human trials found.
currentQuick:
Sake lees is the solid leftover from sake brewing and has long been a Japanese food. It also appears in masks and creams sold for brightening.
Benefits are mainly reported by users; no clinical trials for appearance were found.
How it works: Freeze-dried kasu is reported to contain a tyrosinase-inhibiting extract and antioxidants; tyrosinase is involved in melanin production.
Risks and caveats: Kasu contains alcohol, and sunscreen is advised in the Wikipedia article for users of masks. No safety trials in skin care were found.
deepLead:
Sake lees, known in Japanese as sake kasu, is the white pressed residue left after sake is drawn from fermented rice mash; it typically contains around 8 percent alcohol. It is used in Japanese cooking and, in skin care, in face masks, bath powder and creams marketed for brightening and moisture.
The Wikipedia article attributes claimed skin benefits mostly to user reports and to antioxidants in the masks, and notes that freeze-dried kasu contains an extract that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme involved in pigment production. No clinical trials in the sources reviewed tested it for appearance.

name: Citric acid

angle.text: Citric acid appears in cosmetics as a pH adjuster and in some chemical peels as an alpha hydroxy acid for smoother, brighter skin. Its exfoliating use is common in formulations, while skin-specific trials of citric acid itself are scarce.

summary: A common food acid and cosmetic pH adjuster that is also an AHA peel ingredient, with little skin-specific trial data.
note: Irritant at high concentration.
currentQuick:
Citric acid occurs in citrus fruit and is used everywhere from food to cleaning products. In skin care it mainly adjusts formula pH, and it is also listed among alpha hydroxy acids used in peels.
No controlled trials of citric acid alone as a lightening or resurfacing agent were found.
How it works: As an AHA it is an acid that can exfoliate; as a buffer it sets product pH, and its citrate form binds metal ions.
Risks and caveats: Pure citric acid irritates skin and eyes at concentration, and repeated exposure can erode tooth enamel. It is GRAS in the US and E330 in the EU as a food additive.
deepLead:
Citric acid is a weak organic acid found naturally in citrus fruits and an intermediate in the Krebs cycle. It is widely used as a food acidulant (E330 in the EU) and, in cosmetics, as a pH adjuster; it is also classified as an alpha hydroxy acid and is an active ingredient in some chemical peels.
Pure citric acid is a skin and eye irritant, and concentrated solutions can cause redness and pain. The sources reviewed contain no completed controlled trials of citric acid as a stand-alone skin lightening or resurfacing agent.

name: Trichloroacetic acid peel

chain: Old skin sheds, new skin forms
angle.text: TCA peels are done in clinics to improve sun-damaged skin, melasma, acne marks and scars, giving a fresher, more even surface after healing. Small clinical trials have studied these uses, particularly photodamage, melasma and acne.

summary: A medium-depth clinical peel acid studied in small trials for photodamage, melasma and acne, with real burn and scarring risk.
note: Medium peels are performed by medical providers; risks include scarring and pigment change.
currentQuick:
TCA peels use trichloroacetic acid to injure and renew the skin and are classed as medium-depth. They are used by clinicians for photodamage, pigment problems, acne and scars.
Published human studies exist but are mostly small.
How it works: TCA is a strong acid that precipitates skin proteins, causing controlled injury; depth depends on concentration and technique.
Risks and caveats: ECHA lists severe skin burns and eye damage. Peel complications include prolonged redness, pigment changes, scarring and thinning. Wikipedia says medium peels must be done by a medical provider.
deepLead:
A trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel is a chemical peel using TCA, a strong acid, to cause controlled injury and shedding of the skin; it is described as a medium-depth peel usually done in a doctor's office or outpatient surgery centre. It is used for photodamage, pigment disorders such as melasma, acne and scars, and actinic keratoses.
Published trials are mostly small. Reports describe TCA compared with ascorbic acid combinations in melasma, with 5-ALA photodynamic therapy in actinic keratosis, and as part of combination peels. Risks include pigment changes, scarring and prolonged redness.

name: Lactobionic acid

angle.text: Lactobionic acid is sold as a gentle polyhydroxy acid in skincare, used for smoother, hydrated skin with less stinging than stronger acids. Its chemistry and use in organ-transplant solutions are well documented; published skin trials are few.

summary: A lactose-derived sugar acid sold as a gentle, humectant 'PHA' in skincare, with plenty of chemistry and transplant-medicine use but almost no published skin trials.
note: Skin-specific human trial data are sparse; most published work concerns organ preservation and drug delivery.
currentQuick:
Lactobionic acid is a sugar acid made by oxidising lactose. In cosmetics it is grouped with the polyhydroxy acids (PHAs), a family marketed as milder alternatives to glycolic and lactic acid, and it is described as moisturising and antioxidant.
Most of the published literature on it is about other things: organ-preservation fluids, food additives and nanoparticle drug carriers. Skincare claims rest mainly on manufacturer and review-article descriptions rather than large trials.
How it works: Its many hydroxyl groups let it bind water (humectant) and chelate metals such as iron, which is the basis of its described antioxidant effect. It is a large molecule, which proponents say explains slower skin penetration and lower irritation.
Risks and caveats: Topical products using it are generally described as well tolerated. As with other exfoliating acids, sun protection is advised on labels. Its approved medical roles (organ-preservation solutions, erythromycin lactobionate salt) are unrelated to cosmetic use.
deepLead:
Lactobionic acid (LBA) is a disaccharide sugar acid formed from galactose linked to gluconic acid, and can be made by oxidising lactose. It is freely soluble in water and forms salts with calcium, potassium, sodium and zinc.
In skincare it is classed as a polyhydroxy acid (PHA), marketed as a gentler relative of alpha hydroxy acids, and is described as having moisturising and antioxidant properties. Outside cosmetics, its salts are used as a food stabiliser (calcium lactobionate, E399), in organ-preservation solutions, and as the counter-ion in intravenous erythromycin.
No published randomised trial in the sources reviewed tests lactobionic acid specifically for appearance outcomes. Claims about skin benefits are drawn mainly from descriptive and in-vitro literature.

name: Gluconolactone

chain: Dead cells loosen with low irritation
angle.text: Gluconolactone is a polyhydroxy acid in skincare, used for gentle exfoliation by people whose skin reacts to glycolic acid. Small trials suggest it irritates less than glycolic acid while improving texture; the evidence base is limited.

summary: A food-additive-turned-skincare 'PHA' that small trials suggest irritates less than glycolic acid, though the evidence base is thin.
note: Skin trial evidence is limited to a handful of small studies; products still carry general exfoliant sun-protection advice.
currentQuick:
Gluconolactone (glucono-delta-lactone) is an oxidised derivative of glucose, widely used as a food additive (E575). In skincare it is sold as a polyhydroxy acid, pitched at sensitive skin as a gentler alternative to glycolic acid.
Published skin studies are few. They report effects broadly comparable to alpha hydroxy acids in small comparisons, with less stinging in some, and an expert panel has judged it safe at cosmetic-use levels.
How it works: In water it partly converts to gluconic acid, so acidity develops gradually. It is described as a mild exfoliant, humectant and chelating agent, with some in-vitro data on reduced UV-induced elastin damage.
Risks and caveats: Cosmetic Ingredient Review concluded in 2022 it is safe at reported use concentrations, per Grokipedia. Large oral doses act as a laxative. As with other exfoliating acids, sun protection is generally advised.
deepLead:
Gluconolactone, also called glucono-delta-lactone (GDL), is the cyclic ester of D-gluconic acid, made from glucose oxidation. It is approved as a food additive (E575) used as an acidifier, sequestrant and leavening or curing agent.
In cosmetics it is classed as a polyhydroxy acid (PHA) and used as a skin-conditioning and chelating ingredient, marketed for exfoliation with a lower reported irritation than alpha hydroxy acids. The small clinical literature includes comparisons with glycolic acid and benzoyl peroxide.

name: PHA (polyhydroxy acid)

angle.text: PHAs, mainly gluconolactone and lactobionic acid, are promoted as gentler cousins of AHAs for smoother, brighter skin, including skin that stings easily. The category is largely a marketing and chemical grouping, with sparse published trial data.

summary: A marketing and chemical category of larger-molecule exfoliating acids (gluconolactone, lactobionic acid) pitched as the gentle cousins of AHAs, with sparse trial data.
note: The class is defined mostly by manufacturers and review articles; few independent trials exist.
currentQuick:
Polyhydroxy acids are acids with several hydroxyl groups, used in skincare as exfoliants and humectants. The best-known are gluconolactone and lactobionic acid.
They are marketed as lower-irritation alternatives to glycolic acid for sensitive skin. Evidence consists of a few small comparisons and safety assessments rather than large trials.
How it works: Their larger molecular size is said to slow penetration, and their many hydroxyl groups bind water and metal ions, giving moisturising and antioxidant behaviour alongside mild exfoliation.
Risks and caveats: Described as well tolerated. Regulators say AHAs in general can raise sunburn likelihood, and sun protection is commonly advised on labels.
deepLead:
Polyhydroxy acids (PHAs) are a group of organic acids that carry multiple hydroxyl groups and are used in cosmetics as mild exfoliants and humectants. The two usually named are gluconolactone and lactobionic acid. Gluconolactone is the lactone of gluconic acid, an oxidised derivative of glucose, and lactobionic acid is a gluconic acid-galactose disaccharide.
Marketing positions PHAs as lower-irritation alternatives to alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic acid. A summary of the small trial literature reports similar performance to AHAs in some measures with less stinging in some comparisons. No larger independent trials were found.

name: Willow bark extract

chain: Mild exfoliation and clearing of pores
angle.text: Willow bark extract is used in skincare as a natural source of salicin, marketed as a gentler salicylic-acid-like ingredient for clearer, smoother skin. Oral trials exist for back and joint pain; skin-specific trials have not been found.

summary: A salicin-rich herbal extract with some oral trial data for back and joint pain, but essentially no trials as a skin ingredient.
note: Contains salicylate precursors; the evidence cited is for oral pain use, not appearance.
currentQuick:
Willow bark extract comes from Salix species and contains salicin, which the body converts to salicylate. It has a long history as a traditional pain and fever remedy and is the historical source of salicylic acid chemistry.
Skincare brands sometimes use it as a 'natural salicylic acid' for acne or exfoliation. The clinical trials found are all oral studies in pain conditions, so skin claims are untested in those sources.
How it works: Salicin is a glucoside; after ingestion it is metabolised to salicylic acid derivatives. Reviews note that polyphenols and flavonoids in the extract may also contribute to anti-inflammatory effects.
Risks and caveats: Salicylates are toxic in excess, and salicylate-containing products carry labelled cautions. Topical cosmetic willow extracts have little dedicated safety literature in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Willow bark extract is a preparation from the bark of willow trees, most often white willow (Salix alba), containing the glucoside salicin along with polyphenols. Salicin was isolated in crystalline form in 1828, and salicylic acid is derived from it chemically.
The extract is used orally in Europe for pain, and in skincare it is promoted as a botanical source of salicylic acid. Published human trials in the sources reviewed concern oral use in low back pain and osteoarthritis, not skin appearance.

name: Birch sap

angle.text: Birch sap is a traditional tonic and hair or freckle wash that now appears in K-beauty serums for hydration and a fresher complexion. Skin evidence is mostly laboratory-level, with little human trial data.

summary: A spring-tapped tree water used traditionally as a tonic and hair or freckle wash, now appearing in K-beauty serums; skin evidence is mostly lab-level.
note: Contact allergy to birch sap has been reported in case literature.
currentQuick:
Birch sap is a clear, slightly sweet liquid tapped from birch trees at the end of winter. It is drunk fresh or fermented in northern Europe and Asia and has folk uses for health, hair washing and fading freckles.
It appears as a hydrating ingredient in some skincare. The sources reviewed contain no human trials of its appearance effects; there is a 2024 laboratory-focused paper on skin whitening and an older report of contact allergy.
How it works: It is more than 99% water with small amounts of sugars, minerals such as manganese, amino acids and other plant compounds, which proponents cite for hydrating and antioxidant effects.
Risks and caveats: Birch pollen-allergic people may react; a 1980 report described immediate contact allergy to birch leaves and sap. Tapping can damage trees.
deepLead:
Birch sap, also called birch water, is the liquid tapped from birch trees such as Betula pendula and B. pubescens during the spring thaw. It is clear, slightly sweet and consumed fresh or fermented across boreal regions.
Wikipedia records folk cosmetic uses in several countries, most commonly washing hair, and also against freckles, for hair growth and for skin lightening, and describes these as folk uses rather than established treatments. In modern cosmetics it is used as a hydrating base ingredient.
No human clinical trial of birch sap on appearance was found in the sources reviewed.

name: Erythromycin topical

angle.text: Topical erythromycin is a long-standing prescription treatment for acne, used to reduce acne bacteria and inflamed spots for clearer skin. Acne is its labelled use, and reviews list it alongside clindamycin among common topical antimicrobials.

summary: Old-school topical macrolide antibiotic for acne, labelled for that use only.
note: Prescription antibiotic; label warns of local irritation and rare colitis reports.
currentQuick:
Topical erythromycin is a prescription antibiotic solution applied to the skin for acne. The US label lists acne vulgaris as its indication.
Reviews of acne treatment include it among the commonly used topical antimicrobials, next to clindamycin.
How it works: It is an antibiotic that suppresses acne-associated skin bacteria; reviews also describe non-antimicrobial effects of topical antimicrobials generally.
Risks and caveats: The label lists dryness, peeling, itching, redness and oiliness, and warns that colitis has been reported with antibacterials generally. Pregnancy data in humans are inadequate.
deepLead:
Topical erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic applied to the skin, most commonly as a 2% solution, whose US-labelled indication is the topical treatment of acne vulgaris. It acts against skin bacteria such as Propionibacterium acnes (now Cutibacterium acnes), and reviews of topical acne antimicrobials list erythromycin alongside clindamycin as commonly used agents.
Beyond acne, small older reports have described erythromycin solution used with a topical corticosteroid in perioral dermatitis. Its label lists local reactions such as peeling, dryness, itching, redness and oiliness, and warns that pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents.
Little looksmaxxing-community material was found for this entry; it appears in an appearance context because of acne.

name: Minocycline foam

angle.text: Minocycline foam is a prescription topical antibiotic used for clearer skin in acne and reduced bumps and redness in rosacea. A 4% foam was studied for acne and a 1.5% foam for rosacea in Phase 3 trials.

summary: Prescription minocycline foam trialled in Phase 3 for acne (4%) and rosacea (1.5%).
note: Prescription antibiotic; not an over-the-counter product.
currentQuick:
Topical minocycline foam is a prescription antibiotic foam for acne (4%) and papulopustular rosacea (1.5%).
Both strengths were tested in multiple randomized, vehicle-controlled Phase 3 trials.
How it works: It delivers the tetracycline antibiotic minocycline directly to the skin, aiming to limit systemic exposure compared with the oral drug.
Risks and caveats: Specific adverse-event figures are in the trial reports. It is a prescription antibiotic; oral minocycline is a distinct, systemic product.
deepLead:
Topical minocycline foam is a prescription formulation of the tetracycline antibiotic minocycline, developed to deliver the drug to the skin while limiting systemic exposure. A 4% foam (FMX101) was studied for moderate-to-severe acne vulgaris, and a 1.5% foam (FMX103) for papulopustular rosacea.
Phase 3 randomized, vehicle-controlled trials of 12 weeks were run for both conditions. A pharmacokinetic comparison examined once-daily 4% foam against oral minocycline in acne.
The US FDA approved the 4% foam for acne in 2019 and the 1.5% foam for rosacea in 2020. No looksmaxxing-community material was found for this entry; it appears here because of its use on acne and rosacea.

name: Ivermectin cream

angle.text: Ivermectin cream is a prescription treatment used to reduce the red bumps of papulopustular rosacea for a calmer-looking face. It is approved for this use and backed by Phase 3 trials.

summary: Prescription antiparasitic cream approved for rosacea bumps, backed by Phase 3 trials.
note: Prescription product; unrelated to oral ivermectin use debates.
currentQuick:
Ivermectin 1% cream (Soolantra) is a prescription once-daily topical for papulopustular rosacea.
It has been compared against metronidazole cream in a large Phase 3 trial and reviewed in a meta-analysis.
How it works: It is thought to act on Demodex mites and to reduce inflammatory signals such as LL-37 and KLK5 in the skin.
Risks and caveats: Adverse-event details are in the trial and label data. It is a prescription topical, distinct from oral ivermectin.
deepLead:
Ivermectin 1% (10 mg/g) cream, marketed as Soolantra, is a topical antiparasitic approved for papulopustular rosacea. It is applied once daily to the face.
Researchers have proposed that it acts both on Demodex mites and through anti-inflammatory effects; laboratory work found it reduced expression of the innate-immune mediators LL-37 and KLK5 in skin models. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined its efficacy and quality-of-life impact.
No looksmaxxing-community material was found for this entry; it appears here because of rosacea redness and bumps.

name: Quassia amara extract

angle.text: A 4% quassia gel has been tried for rosacea and facial seborrheic dermatitis, aimed at reducing visible redness and flaking. Two small studies have examined it; larger trials have not been reported.

summary: Herbal 4% gel tried in two small studies for rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.
note: Evidence rests on one small open-label study and one small comparative trial.
currentQuick:
Quassia amara extract is a plant extract made into a 4% gel and tested in rosacea and facial seborrheic dermatitis.
The human evidence is two small studies, one of them open-label.
How it works: Researchers cite reported antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory properties of the plant.
Risks and caveats: Tolerability findings are in the original reports; no wider safety or regulatory data were found.
deepLead:
Quassia amara is a tropical shrub of the Simaroubaceae family whose extracts have been reported to have antiparasitic and anti-inflammatory properties. A topical gel containing 4% quassia extract has been tested in small clinical studies in rosacea and facial seborrheic dermatitis.
The evidence is limited to a 30-patient open-label rosacea study and a 60-patient randomized comparison in seborrheic dermatitis. Other published work is in rats.
No looksmaxxing-community material was found for this entry.

name: Cimetidine for acne

angle.text: Cimetidine, a stomach-acid drug, was tried off-label for acne decades ago because of its weak antiandrogen activity, by mouth and as a lotion. Supporting evidence for this acne use is limited.

summary: An old stomach-acid drug with weak antiandrogen activity that was tried for acne decades ago, with little supporting evidence.
note: Inhibits many drug-metabolizing enzymes; acne evidence is limited to small, dated studies.
currentQuick:
Cimetidine is an H2 blocker used for ulcers and heartburn. A few studies in the late 1970s and 1980s looked at it for acne because it can weakly block androgen receptors.
One small topical study reported generally good results in ten patients, while a 1980 Lancet paper reported no effect of the oral drug. No modern trials were found.
How it works: It blocks stomach H2 receptors and, at high doses, weakly blocks androgen receptors. It also inhibits liver enzymes and can raise estrogen levels.
Risks and caveats: Usually mild effects such as diarrhea and dizziness; gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction at higher doses; many drug interactions. Acne use is off-label.
deepLead:
Cimetidine is a histamine H2 receptor antagonist developed at Smith, Kline & French in the 1970s to reduce stomach acid, and it is sold in many countries for ulcers and heartburn. Because it has a weak ability to block androgen receptors at high doses, it has occasionally been tried as an off-label treatment for acne, both by mouth and as a topical lotion.
The published evidence on acne is small and dated. A 1979 Lancet report and a 1980 Lancet paper titled "Lack of effect of cimetidine in acne" are among the early items, and a 1986 German-language pilot study of a 2% topical lotion in ten patients reported generally good clinical results, with comedones responding best and pustules hardly reduced. Wikipedia describes its androgen-blocking effect as too weak to help much with acne or hirsutism, and the drug is not recommended for those uses.

name: Chlormadinone acetate pill

angle.text: Combined pills containing chlormadinone acetate, sold in places like Germany and Brazil, are used in some countries for androgen-related acne and excess hair. Acne is an off-label or regional use, and little acne-specific trial data has been found.

summary: A European antiandrogenic progestin in combined birth-control pills, used for acne in some countries with little published acne-specific trial data found.
note: Prescription-only; not sold in the US, UK, Canada or Australia.
currentQuick:
Chlormadinone acetate is a progestin with antiandrogen activity, combined with ethinylestradiol in pills such as Belara. It is used for contraception and for androgen-related skin conditions in countries where it is sold.
No acne-specific trials turned up in the sources reviewed; registered studies concern weight change and PCOS.
How it works: It blocks androgen receptors (about 30 to 40 percent of cyproterone acetate affinity) and suppresses LH and FSH, lowering testosterone.
Risks and caveats: Menstrual irregularity, headache, nausea and breast tenderness; contraindicated in pregnancy. Prescription only and unavailable in several countries including the US.
deepLead:
Chlormadinone acetate (CMA) is a synthetic progestin with antiandrogenic activity, used in combined oral contraceptives with ethinylestradiol such as Belara, which is sold in Germany and Brazil. Because it blocks androgen receptors and lowers LH and FSH, such pills are used in some countries for androgen-related skin conditions including acne and hirsutism.
Published trial information specific to acne is limited in the material reviewed. Registered studies compare body-weight change on Belara versus a drospirenone pill and examine hormonal contraceptives in polycystic ovary syndrome, but neither is an acne trial.

name: Drospirenone pill

angle.text: Drospirenone combined pills such as Yasmin and Yaz are indicated for moderate acne in some regions, used for clearer skin through their antiandrogen action. Much of the published research focuses on PCOS.

summary: An antiandrogenic birth-control progestin that is indicated for moderate acne in some regions, with most published research focused on PCOS.
note: Raises potassium and carries a venous clot risk; prescription only.
currentQuick:
Drospirenone is a progestin in contraceptive pills such as Yasmin and Yaz. Because it also blocks androgen receptors, the ethinylestradiol combination is indicated for moderate acne in some jurisdictions.
The studies in the sources reviewed are mostly in PCOS and contraception rather than acne itself.
How it works: It suppresses ovulation as a progestin, blocks androgen receptors, and blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor like spironolactone.
Risks and caveats: Combined pills raise clot risk; some studies suggest higher risk than levonorgestrel pills. Drospirenone can raise potassium. Prescription only.
deepLead:
Drospirenone is a progestin and antiandrogen related to spironolactone, patented in 1976 by Schering AG and introduced as a combined pill with ethinylestradiol around 2000. It is sold as Yasmin, Yaz and generics, and is also used in progestin-only and estetrol combination pills. Wikipedia notes the low-dose ethinylestradiol/drospirenone pill is indicated for moderate acne in some jurisdictions, alongside premenstrual disorders.
Clinical research in the available sources centers on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where a systematic review compared drospirenone pills with other treatments. Documented risks include venous thromboembolism and, with drospirenone, raised potassium.

name: Ruxolitinib cream

angle.text: Ruxolitinib cream is a prescription JAK-inhibitor approved for vitiligo repigmentation and for atopic dermatitis, used to even out patchy skin tone. Phase 3 trials support both approvals.

summary: A prescription JAK-inhibitor cream approved for vitiligo repigmentation and eczema, backed by phase 3 trials.
note: Prescription-only; oral JAK inhibitors carry serious-infection warnings.
currentQuick:
Ruxolitinib cream (Opzelura) is a topical JAK inhibitor approved in the US for atopic dermatitis (2021) and vitiligo (2022).
For vitiligo it has phase 2 and two phase 3 randomized trials behind it, making it one of the better-studied treatments for skin repigmentation.
How it works: It inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 enzymes, damping the immune signaling involved in vitiligo and eczema.
Risks and caveats: Prescription only. Specific adverse events are listed in trial reports and the label; oral JAK inhibitors carry warnings on infections and blood counts.
deepLead:
Ruxolitinib cream (brand name Opzelura) is a topical Janus kinase (JAK1/JAK2) inhibitor. The US FDA approved it in September 2021 for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis, described as the first topical JAK inhibitor approved in the US, and in July 2022 for vitiligo. Its appearance relevance lies mainly in vitiligo, an autoimmune condition that causes skin depigmentation.
Two phase 3 trials published in 2022 tested it in nonsegmental vitiligo, and two phase 3 trials in 2021 tested it in atopic dermatitis. Trials in other skin conditions are registered or completed.
